title: Museums sector warned of 'acute threat' posed by AI scraping bots
content:
AI scraping poses substantial and unsustainable costs on cultural heritage institutions, which are “existential to the mission of these bodies”.
That’s the warning from a new white paper for policymakers based on research conducted by the University of Edinburgh in 2026 as part of the Ekip (European Cultural and Creative Sectors and Industries Policy Platform) project.
Since 2022, there has been a massive increase in automated bot traffic from AI companies scraping data to train generative AI models. Re:Commons: Renewing the Digital Commons for Cultural Heritage found that these bots are putting a strain on organisations’ digital infrastructure, which in some cases is comparable to cyberattacks.
Intelligent Futures: Understanding the Impact of AI
Take stock of what AI means for your museum at our online event on 9 December
Dealing with over-burdened servers has a knock-on effect on engineering and cloud-based hosting costs, as well as staff members’ time and energy.
“For institutions with shrinking public budgets, these costs divert resources from their core mission,” the report warns. “Paradoxically, institutions are also experiencing a loss of legitimate web traffic [due to AI tools like ChatGPT].”
The negative impact on staff morale is also a risk, which stakeholders in the study describing bot traffic as “overwhelming” and “intense”.
Other risks highlighted in the study include copyright infringement, a general distrust of commercial AI models and a loss of context, provenance and control.
Policy measures
Re:Commons warns that current policy debates about AI scraping bots, dominated by copyright and licensing questions, risk overlooking “the infrastructural and material dimensions of the crisis and the specific vulnerability of publicly funded, commons-based institutions”.
The research, undertaken with 115 cultural heritage stakeholders, found that while there is a willingness to share data with AI companies, the combination of unsustainable traffic and lack of dialogue with the companies using the bots has led to reactive measures such as bot-blocking firewalls.
“These defensive responses are quietly creating new enclosures that undermine the very openness that cultural heritage institutions seek to protect,” the report warns.
The paper offers recommendations that aim to not only mitigate the costs of AI bots but also “reimagine AI and the commons on more equitable terms”.
These include:
- Developing and adopting machine-readable rights-reservation standards.
- Requiring AI companies to offer routes to recourse for unlawfully scraped content and to uphold data protection and right to erasure
- Mandating bot identification, redress and transparency pathways.
- Establishing compensation mechanisms that pay for infrastructure rather than merely licensing content.
- Investing in shared, sovereign, environmentally sustainable public digital infrastructure.
- Supporting small-scale, community-governed and public-interest AI models aligned with the values of cultural heritage.
  What are museums doing to mitigate the impact of AI bots?
According to the research undertaken by the University of Edinburgh, organisations have been forced to “act alone” to deploy some of the following defensive measures to protect their infrastructure:
- Server upgrades “This is a reactive strategy that treats symptoms rather than causes, available only to institutions with the budgets to sustain it,” the report’s authors note.
- IP blocking and rate limiting “These measures are blunt and error-prone,” the report states.
- Third-party firewall services “In defending themselves against one form of private extraction, institutions become dependent on another set of intermediaries that now sit between the public and public cultural heritage,” the authors say.
- Whack-a-mole and the blocking paradox The research found mitigation strategies shift as bots learn to get around the above measures but warns: “Blocking also often fails to achieve its aim.”
The reports authors are: Caitlin McDonald, Morgan Currie, Lara Dal Molin, Nicola Osborne, Anna Talley, Matea Senkić, and Jennifer Volk.
The research team has contributed to two European Commission policy calls for evidence, on the impact of AI scraping bots on the gallery, library, archives and museum (GLAM) sector and on copyright environment for cultural heritage institutions in relation to scraping by AI companies.

report.summary: A University of Edinburgh white paper warns AI scraping bots impose unsustainable infrastructure costs and existential risks on museums, urging policy action beyond copyright.
report.background: Since 2022, generative AI companies have dramatically increased automated scraping of web data to train models. Cultural heritage institutions—museums, galleries, libraries and archives—depend on open digital access but often run on shrinking public budgets. The Re:Commons white paper, based on University of Edinburgh research for the Ekip project and 115 stakeholder interviews, finds that current policy debates focus heavily on copyright and licensing while overlooking the material costs of bot traffic. Institutions face overloaded servers, higher cloud bills, staff burnout and, paradoxically, less legitimate traffic as users turn to AI chatbots. The report argues that publicly funded, commons-based institutions are uniquely vulnerable and that defensive responses may undermine the openness they exist to protect.
key_points: AI scraping traffic is straining museum digital infrastructure in ways comparable to cyberattacks. Overloaded servers raise cloud hosting and engineering costs and consume staff time, diverting scarce resources from core missions. Stakeholders described bot traffic as overwhelming and intense, with negative effects on morale. The report warns that for institutions facing shrinking public budgets, these costs are not merely operational but existential to their public-interest mission.

Museums are responding alone with reactive measures: server upgrades, IP blocking, rate limiting and third-party firewalls. The report calls these approaches blunt, error-prone and symptomatic rather than causal. Third-party firewalls create new dependencies between the public and public cultural heritage, while blocking often fails as bots adapt. These defensive responses risk creating new enclosures that undermine the openness cultural institutions seek to protect.

The white paper urges policymakers to require bot identification, transparency and redress pathways, plus routes to recourse for unlawfully scraped content and data protection or erasure rights. It also recommends machine-readable rights-reservation standards and compensation mechanisms that fund infrastructure rather than merely licensing content. Longer-term proposals include shared, sovereign and environmentally sustainable public digital infrastructure and support for small-scale, public-interest AI models aligned with cultural heritage values.

There is willingness among cultural heritage organisations to share data with AI companies, but unsustainable traffic and a lack of dialogue have pushed many toward blocking. The research describes a whack-a-mole dynamic in which mitigation strategies shift as bots learn to evade them. The report warns that blocking often fails to achieve its aim while still damaging legitimate access and institutional openness.

The research team contributed to two European Commission policy calls for evidence—on AI scraping bots’ impact on the GLAM sector and on the copyright environment for cultural heritage institutions. The report argues that a copyright-only framing misses the infrastructural and material dimensions of the crisis and the specific vulnerability of publicly funded, commons-based institutions.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the report signals growing scrutiny of crawling practices and demands for bot identification, transparency, recourse and infrastructure compensation. Developers may face stricter technical and policy expectations around polite crawling, rights reservation and data provenance. Regular users could see more cultural content locked behind bot-blocking systems, reducing the open web’s richness. Museums may continue retreating from openness to protect servers, weakening the digital commons. The broader lesson is that AI training data is not free: its infrastructure costs fall on public institutions unless policymakers create equitable scraping, licensing and compensation frameworks.
report.tools: Watch machine-readable rights-reservation standards and bot-identification efforts. For hands-on mitigation, test open-source Anubis, a proof-of-work bot filter, and CrowdSec or fail2ban for rate limiting and blocking. Review robots.txt and emerging AI.txt conventions. Commercial options include Cloudflare bot management and AI crawl controls. Museums should also monitor European policy work on GLAM scraping and public-interest AI infrastructure.
